preEngineeredClimb.description: A module bought already engineered can be taken further at an engineer, and `applyBlueprint` accepts its Operations id on the module that is sold carrying it even though no engineering menu lists one. The Mercenary Module Reinforcement Package is the case that proves the route: it has no menu at all. It arrives at grade 1, so its recipe defines grades 2-5 only — asking for grade 1 is asking to recreate the purchase, which no recipe can do.

scannerIdCollision.description: One journal `BlueprintName`, two recipes. The game writes `Sensor_LongRange` and `Sensor_WideAngle` for both the internal sensor suite's modification and the KWS/manifest/wake scanners', and the two roll different stats in opposite directions — Long Range costs the suite mass and the scanner power draw, Wide Angle the reverse. `blueprints.jsonc` keys the scanner side under `Scanner_LongRange` / `Scanner_WideAngle`, the spelling the scanner menus list, so which numbers apply is a fact about the fitted module and not about the id. The top-level `journalNames` pins the blueprint side of this and of every other id of the shape. Resolution is those facts read against a module's menu, so an implementation needs no third list. Each case pins the same id on both families at the same grade and quality: `resolved` is the `BLUEPRINTS` key the module rolls, `modifiers` the exact `Engineering.Modifiers` block that follows. The corpus entry this comes from is a wake scanner declaring `Sensor_LongRange` at grade 3 (`type9-military-combat-3`, an EDSY-authored build). `refused` pins the direction the resolution does not run: a sensor suite is not thereby offered the scanner's id.

overchargedIdCollision.description: The same shape as `scannerIdCollision` and by far the commoner case: the game writes `Weapon_Overcharged` for every weapon's Overcharged, but a multi-cannon's also cuts the clip 3-15% and the others' does not, so `blueprints.jsonc` keys the multi-cannon side under `MC_Overcharged` — the spelling the multi-cannon menus list. 70 of the build corpus's 1902 declared entries need this resolution, against one for the scanners. Each case pins the id as a journal writes it, the `BLUEPRINTS` key the fitted module actually rolls, and the exact `Engineering.Modifiers` block that follows at the pinned grade and quality. The cannon case is the control: same id, same three legs, and no `AmmoClipSize` — which is also where https://github.com/DarkSession/Elite-Dangerous-Almanac/issues/48 lives, EDSY holding that a cannon's clip should drop here too. If that is ever settled in EDSY's favour this case is what has to change, deliberately.

journalSpellings.description: Journal `EngineerModifications` spellings read off a real `StoredModules` capture (521 stored modules, contributed by the repository owner 2026-08-07 UTC; scrubbed of the commander, carrier and market it came from, which say nothing about the game). Of the 46 distinct spellings in that capture, 43 resolve against `BLUEPRINTS` and the other three are the `Decorative_*` liveries, which name no recipe at all and are pinned in §decorativeModifications. These are the cases worth pinning: an id whose key is not what the game writes, and one whose journal spelling the catalogue had missed entirely. `resolved` is what `resolveBlueprintForModule` answers — the `BLUEPRINTS` key the fitted module actually rolls, returned in the caller’s own casing, since every lookup downstream matches case-insensitively.

cases.note: The game writes the module spelling on a Guardian *weapon*. Both registry spellings resolve to the same recipe.
The game writes this one lower-case. Every lookup matches case-insensitively, so it resolves to `Weapon_LongRange` without being rewritten.

operationsKeys.description: Operations blueprints are keyed as the registry publishes them minus Inara’s `recipe_` prefix — neither coriolis (81 keys, none prefixed) nor EDSY (no `recipe_` string at all) uses it, and no observed build does either. `prefixed` is the whole of the exception: two declared Inara aliases for a recipe whose real name, `GuardianModule_Sturdy`, is a key in its own right. `observed` records a spelling read off a real Inara SLEF export contributed by the repository owner — a Mercenary Module Reinforcement Package taken to grade 5, which before the prefix was dropped resolved to nothing and made `applyBlueprint` throw on a genuine build. The export writes it `modulereinforcement_heavyduty`; `blueprint` below is the catalogue key that id resolves to, whose casing comes from a raw journal rather than from Inara, which lower-cases everything it exports. Every lookup matches case-insensitively, so both forms reach the same record.

decorativeModifications.description: The festive transformations the game writes in the same journal field as an engineering blueprint, read off the same `StoredModules` capture as §journalSpellings — it holds three medium turreted Remote Release Flak Launchers, one per colour. They are not engineering: no grade, no materials, and no engineer offers one. So they are absent from `BLUEPRINTS` and from every menu in `engineering-options`, and `DECORATIVE_MODIFICATIONS` is what makes the id resolve to something rather than to nothing — the distinction between "this id is real and names no recipe" and "this id is unknown", which is the whole reason the catalogue exists. They are not cosmetic-only either: a festive launcher fires fireworks rather than flak, and every one of them carries a single `Damage` modifier of -99%, so no record here may be read as "this module is unmodified". `module` is the only module observed carrying one, and the catalogue groups it nowhere: a Remote Release Flak Launcher takes no engineering, and being awarded one already transformed does not make it engineerable. `name` pairs the festive naming with the id's colour; no registry publishes the outfitting panel's own string.

resolved.description: What the stored modifier makes of the medium turreted Remote Release Flak Launcher, and the outfitting-panel reading it was derived from. The panel is rounded to one decimal, so it does not pin the modifier on its own — but the three figures together do: -99.0% of the 34 base damage is 0.34, which displays as 0.3, and 0.34 x the 0.5 rate of fire is 0.17, which displays as 0.2/s. An overwrite to a flat 0.3 would read -99.1% and 0.1/s, so the modifier is multiplicative and the panel's 0.3 is a rounding. Recomputing these is what would catch the modifier being re-entered as the displayed value.

journalNames.description: Every `BLUEPRINTS` record whose key is NOT the `BlueprintName` the game writes, mapped to the id it is written as. Three of the 109; of the rest, 79 are already the journal id and 27 are Operations keys for which no journal spelling has been observed, which is why the field is absent from them. Each of the three shares its journal id with another record that rolls different numbers, so reading the id alone would fold the wrong recipe: the two scanner ids are §scannerIdCollision, and `MC_Overcharged` is the multi-cannon Overcharged, which cuts the clip by 3-15% where the `Weapon_Overcharged` every other weapon menu lists leaves it alone. `resolveBlueprintForModule` settles each by asking which recipe the fitted module's own menu offers.

reachability.description: Which ids `applyBlueprint` accepts on at least one module, swept over every id in `BLUEPRINTS` and `EXPERIMENTAL_EFFECTS` against all 1197 module symbols. Every blueprint reaches a module; one experimental effect reaches none, and `unreachableBlueprints` / `unreachableExperimentals` are that residue in full — whole lists rather than spot checks, so an id stranded by a later change fails a test instead of passing unnoticed. `reachable` pins the six blueprints whose route to a module is narrow enough to lose by accident: each on a module that accepts it, one that must refuse it, and the exact count that takes it, so a menu row widened into a neighbouring family fails here rather than satisfying the sweep by reaching everything.
